memory_candidates.content: When a guard/wrapper script needs to REPLAY a prior invocation's exact stdout/stderr bytes later (result-sharing caches, retry-with-cached-output patterns), capture stdout and stderr to SEPARATE files via `cmd > >(tee out) 2> >(tee err >&2)` plus a trailing bare `wait` (to let both async tee subshells flush before reading the capture files) rather than one merged log. This preserves per-stream byte-for-byte transparency (a caller's own `2>&1` or separate stdout/stderr capture is still exactly reproduced) while still letting you build a human-readable combined log by concatenating the two afterward.

GNU `stat -c '%Y'` (mtime in whole seconds) is not fine-grained enough for a fast edit-then-rebuild content-fingerprint check: two writes within the same wall-clock second can produce an identical (size, mtime-seconds) tuple even with different content, causing a false 'unchanged' verdict. Use `stat -c '%y'` (nanosecond-resolution formatted timestamp) instead on any filesystem that records sub-second mtimes (ext4/xfs/btrfs/tmpfs all do) to close this gap cheaply, without needing to fall back to full content hashing.

systemd unit properties like MemoryHigh=/MemoryMax= accept native percentage-of-total values (e.g. `MemoryHigh=60%`) directly on the `systemd-run -p` command line -- no need to compute an absolute byte figure from /proc/meminfo yourself. This is the simplest way to satisfy a 'never hardcode a machine-specific byte constant' requirement for cgroup memory bounding.
